questions.stem:
a) List the four classes of antihypertensive agents recommended as first-line therapy for uncomplicated hypertension according to the 2023 ESH/ESC guidelines. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug. (2 marks)
c) Briefly explain why beta blockers are no longer recommended as first-line therapy in uncomplicated hypertension. (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four classes of antihypertensive agents recommended as first-line therapy for uncomplicated hypertension are:
   - Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine)
   - ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril)
   - Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) (e.g., losartan)
   - Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide)

b) Examples of drugs in each class:
   - Calcium channel blockers: Amlodipine
   - ACE inhibitors: Lisinopril
   - ARBs: Losartan
   - Thiazide diuretics: Hydrochlorothiazide

c) Beta blockers are no longer recommended as first-line therapy in uncomplicated hypertension due to their inferior protection against stroke and heart failure compared to other classes, and their association with increased risk of new-onset diabetes.

questions.stem:
a) List the three primary mechanisms by which loop diuretics exert their diuretic effect. (1.5 marks)
b) Provide two examples of loop diuretics. (1 mark)
c) Describe two adverse effects associated with chronic loop diuretic use. (2.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three primary mechanisms by which loop diuretics exert their diuretic effect are:
   - Inhibition of the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
   - Increased excretion of sodium, chloride, and water
   - Increased excretion of potassium, calcium, and magnesium

b) Examples of loop diuretics:
   - Furosemide
   - Bumetanide

c) Adverse effects associated with chronic loop diuretic use:
   - Hypokalemia: Loop diuretics increase urinary potassium excretion, leading to low serum potassium levels, which can cause muscle weakness, cramps, and cardiac arrhythmias.
   - Metabolic alkalosis: Volume depletion and hypochloremia lead to contraction alkalosis, which can cause symptoms such as confusion, nausea, and vomiting.

questions.stem:
a) List the four classes of antiarrhythmic drugs according to the Vaughan Williams classification. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug. (2 marks)
c) Briefly explain the mechanism of action of class III antiarrhythmics. (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four classes of antiarrhythmic drugs according to the Vaughan Williams classification are:
   - Class I: Sodium channel blockers
   - Class II: Beta blockers
   - Class III: Potassium channel blockers
   - Class IV: Calcium channel blockers

b) Examples of drugs in each class:
   - Class I: Lidocaine
   - Class II: Metoprolol
   - Class III: Amiodarone
   - Class IV: Diltiazem

c) The mechanism of action of class III antiarrhythmics is the blockade of potassium channels, which prolongs the action potential duration and refractory period, thereby suppressing re-entrant arrhythmias.

questions.stem:
a) List the three primary goals of therapy in the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). (1.5 marks)
b) Provide two examples of beta blockers used in the management of HFrEF. (1 mark)
c) Describe two adverse effects associated with beta blocker use in HFrEF. (2.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three primary goals of therapy in the management of HFrEF are:
   - Improve symptoms and quality of life
   - Reduce hospitalizations
   - Prolong survival

b) Examples of beta blockers used in the management of HFrEF:
   - Carvedilol
   - Metoprolol succinate

c) Adverse effects associated with beta blocker use in HFrEF:
   - Bradycardia: Beta blockers slow the heart rate, which can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness, and syncope.
   - Hypotension: Beta blockers reduce blood pressure, which can cause symptoms such as lightheadedness and syncope.

questions.stem:
a) List the four primary classes of lipid-lowering agents. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug. (2 marks)
c) Briefly explain why statins are the first-line therapy for lipid management in most patients. (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four primary classes of lipid-lowering agents are:
   - HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins)
   - Ezetimibe (cholesterol absorption inhibitor)
   - PCSK9 inhibitors
   - Fibrates

b) Examples of drugs in each class:
   - Statins: Atorvastatin
   - Ezetimibe: Ezetimibe
   - PCSK9 inhibitors: Alirocumab
   - Fibrates: Fenofibrate

c) Statins are the first-line therapy for lipid management in most patients due to their proven efficacy in reducing LDL cholesterol, cardiovascular events, and mortality, as well as their favorable safety profile and cost-effectiveness.

questions.stem:
a) List the three primary mechanisms by which ACE inhibitors exert their antihypertensive and cardioprotective effects. (1.5 marks)
b) Provide two examples of ACE inhibitors. (1 mark)
c) Describe two adverse effects associated with ACE inhibitor use. (2.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three primary mechanisms by which ACE inhibitors exert their antihypertensive and cardioprotective effects are:
   - Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), reducing the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
   - Decreased vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion
   - Reduced sodium and water retention

b) Examples of ACE inhibitors:
   - Lisinopril
   - Enalapril

c) Adverse effects associated with ACE inhibitor use:
   - Hyperkalemia: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion, leading to increased serum potassium levels.
   - Dry cough: ACE inhibitors can cause a persistent dry cough due to increased bradykinin levels.

questions.stem:
a) List the three primary classes of anticoagulants. (1.5 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug. (1.5 marks)
c) Briefly explain the mechanism of action of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three primary classes of anticoagulants are:
   - Vitamin K antagonists (e.g., warfarin)
   - Heparins (e.g., unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin)
   - Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)

b) Examples of drugs in each class:
   - Vitamin K antagonists: Warfarin
   - Heparins: Enoxaparin
   - DOACs: Apixaban

c) The mechanism of action of DOACs is the direct inhibition of specific clotting factors:
   - Direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g., dabigatran) inhibit thrombin (factor IIa)
   - Factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., apixaban, rivaroxaban) inhibit factor Xa, preventing the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin.

questions.stem:
a) List the four primary classes of diuretics. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug. (2 marks)
c) Briefly explain why potassium-sparing diuretics are often combined with loop or thiazide diuretics. (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four primary classes of diuretics are:
   - Loop diuretics
   - Thiazide diuretics
   - Potassium-sparing diuretics
   - Osmotic diuretics

b) Examples of drugs in each class:
   - Loop diuretics: Furosemide
   - Thiazide diuretics: Hydrochlorothiazide
   - Potassium-sparing diuretics: Spironolactone
   - Osmotic diuretics: Mannitol

c) Potassium-sparing diuretics are often combined with loop or thiazide diuretics to counteract the potassium-wasting effects of these agents, thereby reducing the risk of hypokalemia.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73m²) presents to the emergency department with a BP of 190/110 mmHg, headache, and blurred vision. His current medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID, and atorvastatin 40 mg nocte.

a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (2 marks)
b) Outline the immediate management of this patient, including pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. (8 marks)
c) What are the long-term management goals for this patient, and how would you monitor his progress? (5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The most likely diagnosis is hypertensive emergency with target organ damage (hypertensive retinopathy and possible hypertensive encephalopathy).

b) Immediate management:
   - Pharmacological interventions:
     1. Administer IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, then 20-80 mg every 10 minutes as needed (goal: reduce MAP by 10-20% in the first hour).
     2. Consider IV nitroglycerin or nicardipine if labetalol is contraindicated or ineffective.
     3. Avoid sublingual nifedipine due to risk of unpredictable BP drops.
     4. Continue home antihypertensives (amlodipine) unless contraindicated.
     5. Monitor BP every 5-15 minutes during acute phase.
   - Non-pharmacological interventions:
     1. Place patient in a quiet, dark room to reduce stimulation.
     2. Ensure continuous cardiac and BP monitoring.
     3. Assess for signs of end-organ damage (e.g., fundoscopy for retinopathy, neurological exam).
     4. Obtain baseline labs (serum creatinine, potassium, CBC, troponin, ECG).

c) Long-term management goals and monitoring:
   - BP target: <130/80 mmHg (KDIGO 2021 guidelines for diabetes and CKD).
   - Glycemic control: HbA1c <7% (ADA guidelines).
   - Lipid control: LDL <1.8 mmol/L (ESC 2019 guidelines).
   - Renal protection: Monitor eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) annually.
   - Monitoring schedule:
     1. BP: Every 1-3 months once stable.
     2. Renal function: Serum creatinine and eGFR every 3-6 months.
     3. Electrolytes: Serum potassium every 3-6 months (due to ACEi/ARB use).
     4. HbA1c: Every 3-6 months.
     5. Lipid profile: Annually or as indicated.
   - Medication adjustments:
     1. Consider adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB for renal protection (e.g., lisinopril 5-10 mg daily).
     2. Add a thiazide-like diuretic (e.g., indapamide) if BP remains uncontrolled.
     3. Optimize diabetes management (e.g., consider SGLT2 inhibitor like empagliflozin for renal and CV benefits).

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old woman with a history of HFrEF (LVEF 25%), hypertension, and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m²) presents to the clinic with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower limb edema. Her current medications include carvedilol 25 mg BID, enalapril 10 mg BID, spironolactone 25 mg daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily. She reports adherence to her medications but continues to experience symptoms.

a) What is the most likely cause of her worsening symptoms? (2 marks)
b) Outline a step-by-step approach to optimizing her pharmacotherapy, including drug adjustments and additions. (10 marks)
c) What non-pharmacological interventions would you recommend for this patient? (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The most likely cause of her worsening symptoms is decompensated heart failure, possibly due to fluid overload and suboptimal diuresis.

b) Step-by-step approach to optimizing pharmacotherapy:
   1. Assess volume status and diuretic response:
      - Check for signs of fluid overload (e.g., weight gain, edema, crackles on lung exam).
      - Consider increasing furosemide to 80 mg BID or adding a thiazide-like diuretic (e.g., metolazone 2.5-5 mg daily) for synergistic diuresis.
   2. Optimize beta blocker therapy:
      - Titrate carvedilol to the maximum tolerated dose (e.g., 50 mg BID) if heart rate and BP allow.
      - Ensure patient is euvolemic before up-titration.
   3. Optimize ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy:
      - Titrate enalapril to the maximum tolerated dose (e.g., 20 mg BID) if BP allows.
      - Consider switching to an ARB (e.g., valsartan) if ACE inhibitor is not tolerated (e.g., due to cough).
   4. Add SGLT2 inhibitor:
      - Start dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or empagliflozin 10 mg daily for additional diuretic and cardioprotective effects.
   5. Consider adding an ARNI (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor):
      - Switch enalapril to sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BID (if BP allows) for improved outcomes.
   6. Consider adding ivabradine:
      - If heart rate remains >70 bpm despite beta blocker optimization, add ivabradine 5 mg BID to reduce heart rate and improve symptoms.
   7. Monitor electrolytes and renal function:
      - Check serum potassium, creatinine, and eGFR 1-2 weeks after any medication changes.
   8. Consider digoxin:
      - Add digoxin 0.125 mg daily if patient remains symptomatic despite optimized therapy (use cautiously in CKD).

c) Non-pharmacological interventions:
   1. Sodium restriction: Advise a sodium-restricted diet (<2 g/day) to reduce fluid retention.
   2. Fluid restriction: Limit fluid intake to 1.5-2 L/day if hyponatremia is present.
   3. Daily weight monitoring: Instruct patient to weigh herself daily and report weight gain >2 kg in 3 days.
   4. Exercise: Encourage moderate exercise (e.g., walking) as tolerated to improve functional capacity.
   5. Smoking cessation and alcohol reduction: Advise smoking cessation and limit alcohol intake.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male with stage 3 CKD (eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73m²) and hypertension presents with BP 158/94 mmHg. His current medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nocte. Which of the following antihypertensives is MOST appropriate to add for BP control while minimizing renal risk?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) are first-line for hypertension in CKD due to renoprotective effects, despite a slight initial rise in creatinine. Thiazides are less effective at eGFR <45, spironolactone risks hyperkalaemia in CKD, and doxazosin is not first-line.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female with NYHA class II heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is currently on carvedilol 12.5 mg BD and furosemide 40 mg BD. Her BP is 102/68 mmHg, HR 58 bpm, and she reports mild dyspnoea on exertion. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: a) Increase carvedilol to 25 mg BD
d) Switch carvedilol to metoprolol succinate
questions.explanation: Spironolactone is recommended in HFrEF patients with persistent symptoms despite ACEI/ARB and beta-blocker therapy (NYHA II-IV) to reduce mortality and hospitalization. Increasing carvedilol risks bradycardia/ hypotension; digoxin is for rate control in AF or symptom control in HFrEF; metoprolol succinate is not superior to carvedilol.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with atrial fibrillation (AF) and CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 3 is admitted for elective knee replacement. His CrCl is 55 mL/min. Which anticoagulant is MOST appropriate for thromboprophylaxis post-surgery?
questions.explanation: LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is preferred for post-surgical thromboprophylaxis in CKD (CrCl 30–59 mL/min) due to predictable pharmacokinetics and no need for monitoring. DOACs require dose adjustment or are contraindicated in moderate CKD; warfarin is less practical perioperatively.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with BP 148/92 mmHg. His HbA1c is 7.8% and LDL-C is 3.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate BP target according to KDIGO guidelines?
questions.explanation: KDIGO recommends a BP target of <130/80 mmHg in patients with diabetes and hypertension to reduce renal and cardiovascular risk. <140/90 is general CKD target; <120/70 is not standard; <150/95 is too lenient.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with chronic AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4) is started on dabigatran 150 mg BD for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter?
questions.explanation: Dabigatran is renally excreted; monitoring eGFR is critical to adjust dose and avoid accumulation. INR is for warfarin; aPTT is not routinely monitored for DOACs; D-dimer is not relevant for AF anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with NYHA class III HFrEF (EF 30%) is on lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. He develops hyperkalaemia (K+ 5.8 mmol/L) and worsening renal function (eGFR 35 mL/min). Which of the following is the MOST appropriate adjustment?
options: a) Stop spironolactone and start eplerenone
b) Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg daily and monitor K+
c) Switch spironolactone to amiloride 5 mg daily
d) Increase lisinopril to 40 mg daily
questions.answer: b) Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg daily and monitor K+
questions.explanation: Reducing spironolactone dose and monitoring K+ is appropriate to manage hyperkalaemia while retaining some mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism benefit. Stopping spironolactone loses mortality benefit; amiloride is not equivalent; increasing lisinopril worsens hyperkalaemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with no comorbidities presents with BP 162/104 mmHg on three separate occasions. Ambulatory BP monitoring confirms daytime average BP 158/98 mmHg. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial antihypertensive therapy?
questions.explanation: Amlodipine (CCB) is a first-line option for uncomplicated hypertension in young adults due to efficacy and tolerability. Thiazides are less effective in normovolaemic patients; ACEI is not first-line unless compelling indications (e.g., diabetes); doxazosin is not first-line.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old male with HFrEF (EF 25%) and CKD stage 4 (eGFR 25 mL/min) is admitted with acute decompensated heart failure. His current medications include furosemide 80 mg BD and carvedilol 12.5 mg BD. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate diuretic adjustment?
options: a) Increase furosemide to 160 mg BD
c) Switch to bumetanide 4 mg BD
questions.explanation: Adding a thiazide-like diuretic (metolazone) enhances diuresis in resistant oedema, especially in CKD where loop diuretic efficacy is reduced. Increasing furosemide may not overcome diuretic resistance; spironolactone risks hyperkalaemia in CKD; bumetanide is not superior to furosemide.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with hypertension and dyslipidaemia is started on atorvastatin 40 mg nocte. His baseline LFTs are normal. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring schedule?
options: a) LFTs at baseline and 6–12 weeks after initiation
d) LFTs annually regardless of symptoms
questions.answer: a) LFTs at baseline and 6–12 weeks after initiation
questions.explanation: Statins require baseline LFTs and repeat at 6–12 weeks to monitor for hepatotoxicity. Monthly monitoring is excessive; monitoring only if symptomatic may miss early elevations; annual monitoring is insufficient.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 2) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 48 mL/min) is started on rivaroxaban 15 mg daily for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate dose adjustment?
questions.explanation: Rivaroxaban requires dose reduction to 15 mg daily (or 10 mg daily if eGFR 15–49 mL/min) for stroke prevention in AF. No adjustment is unsafe in CKD; increasing dose risks bleeding; switching to warfarin is not necessary.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male with hypertension and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 65 mL/min) is started on lisinopril 10 mg daily. His baseline creatinine is 120 µmol/L (eGFR 65 mL/min) and K+ 4.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step after 1 week?
options: a) Repeat creatinine and K+ in 1–2 weeks
b) Increase lisinopril to 20 mg daily
d) Stop lisinopril and switch to losartan
questions.answer: a) Repeat creatinine and K+ in 1–2 weeks
questions.explanation: ACEI/ARB initiation requires monitoring of creatinine and K+ within 1–2 weeks to assess for expected small rise in creatinine and hyperkalaemia. Increasing dose prematurely risks complications; adding another antihypertensive is not necessary; switching to ARB is not indicated unless ACEI intolerance.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female with NYHA class II HFrEF (EF 35%) is on lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. She develops gynaecomastia. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate alternative to spironolactone?
questions.explanation: Eplerenone is a selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with less antiandrogenic effects, making it suitable for patients intolerant to spironolactone due to gynaecomastia. Amiloride lacks mortality benefit; furosemide is not a mineralocorticoid antagonist; digoxin does not address aldosterone effects.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male with hypertension and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 42 mL/min) is started on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is MOST likely to occur?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics increase urinary potassium excretion, leading to hypokalaemia. Hyperkalaemia is unlikely unless combined with ACEI/ARB/ spironolactone; hypercalcaemia and hypernatraemia are not typical.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old female with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3) and CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) is started on apixaban 5 mg BD for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate monitoring parameter?
questions.explanation: Apixaban is renally excreted; monitoring eGFR is critical to adjust dose and avoid accumulation. INR is for warfarin; anti-Xa monitoring is not standard for DOACs; D-dimer is not relevant for AF anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with BP 152/96 mmHg. His current medications include metformin 1 g BD and atorvastatin 40 mg nocte. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial antihypertensive therapy?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) are first-line in diabetes due to renoprotective effects and reduction in cardiovascular events. Thiazides are less effective in normovolaemic diabetics; CCBs are second-line; doxazosin is not first-line.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with HFrEF (EF 20%) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 38 mL/min) is admitted with acute decompensated heart failure. His current medications include furosemide 80 mg BD and carvedilol 12.5 mg BD. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate inotropic agent if he remains hypotensive?
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist used for acute decompensated heart failure with hypotension or cardiogenic shock. Digoxin is for rate control in AF or chronic HFrEF; milrinone and levosimendan are not first-line inotropes due to risk of arrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female with hypertension and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 68 mL/min) is started on losartan 50 mg daily. Her baseline creatinine is 110 µmol/L (eGFR 68 mL/min) and K+ 4.5 mmol/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step after 2 weeks?
options: a) Repeat creatinine and K+ in 1–2 weeks
b) Increase losartan to 100 mg daily
d) Stop losartan and switch to amlodipine
questions.answer: a) Repeat creatinine and K+ in 1���2 weeks
questions.explanation: ARB initiation requires monitoring of creatinine and K+ within 1–2 weeks to assess for expected small rise in creatinine and hyperkalaemia. Increasing dose prematurely risks complications; adding a thiazide may be considered later for BP control; switching to CCB is not necessary unless intolerance.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 45 mL/min) is started on dabigatran 110 mg BD for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate reversal agent in case of major bleeding?
questions.explanation: Idarucizumab is a specific reversal agent for dabigatran. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin; vitamin K reverses warfarin; andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female with hypertension and dyslipidaemia is started on simvastatin 40 mg nocte. Her baseline LFTs are normal. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice regarding grapefruit juice?
questions.explanation: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4, increasing simvastatin levels and risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. Avoidance is recommended. Limiting intake does not eliminate risk.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with HFrEF (EF 30%) and CKD stage 4 (eGFR 28 mL/min) is on lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. He develops hyperkalaemia (K+ 5.9 mmol/L). Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate intervention?
options: a) Stop spironolactone and start calcium polystyrene sulfonate
b) Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg daily and monitor K+
d) Administer intravenous insulin and dextrose
questions.answer: d) Administer intravenous insulin and dextrose
questions.explanation: For severe hyperkalaemia (K+ ≥6.0 mmol/L), immediate measures include IV insulin/dextrose to shift K+ intracellularly. Calcium gluconate is for ECG changes; reducing spironolactone is appropriate but not immediate; calcium polystyrene sulfonate is for non-urgent management.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male with hypertension and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 62 mL/min) is started on amlodipine 5 mg daily. Which of the following is the MOST likely adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Amlodipine (CCB) commonly causes peripheral oedema due to vasodilation. Hyperkalaemia and bradycardia are not typical; hypoglycaemia is unrelated.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 40 mL/min) is started on rivaroxaban 15 mg daily for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice regarding NSAID use?
options: b) Limit to 3 days per week
questions.explanation: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and worsen renal function in CKD. Avoidance is recommended. Limiting use does not eliminate risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with BP 148/94 mmHg. His HbA1c is 8.2% and LDL-C is 3.8 mmol/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate statin intensity?
questions.explanation: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) is recommended for patients with diabetes and additional cardiovascular risk factors. Low/moderate-intensity statins are insufficient.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male with HFrEF (EF 25%) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 35 mL/min) is on lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. He develops worsening renal function (eGFR 25 mL/min) and hyperkalaemia (K+ 5.7 mmol/L). Which of the following is the MOST appropriate adjustment?
options: a) Stop spironolactone and start eplerenone
b) Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg daily and monitor K+
c) Switch spironolactone to amiloride 5 mg daily
d) Stop lisinopril and switch to amlodipine
questions.answer: b) Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg daily and monitor K+
questions.explanation: Reducing spironolactone dose and monitoring K+ is appropriate to manage hyperkalaemia and worsening renal function while retaining some benefit. Stopping spironolactone loses mortality benefit; amiloride is not equivalent; stopping lisinopril risks worsening heart failure.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female with hypertension and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 68 mL/min) is started on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Which of the following is the MOST likely metabolic adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics increase uric acid reabsorption, leading to hyperuricaemia and gout risk. Hyperglycaemia is possible but less likely than hyperuricaemia; hypercalcaemia and hypernatraemia are not typical.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4) and CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) is started on apixaban 5 mg BD for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice regarding herbal supplements?
options: a) Avoid St. John’s wort entirely
questions.answer: a) Avoid St. John’s wort entirely
questions.explanation: St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4 and P-gp, reducing apixaban levels and efficacy. Avoidance is recommended. Other supplements may also interact, but St. John’s wort is a well-known inducer.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male with hypertension and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 65 mL/min) is started on lisinopril 10 mg daily. His baseline creatinine is 120 µmol/L (eGFR 65 mL/min) and K+ 4.3 mmol/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice regarding potassium intake?
options: a) Restrict dietary potassium to <2 g/day
b) No restriction needed unless K+ >5.0 mmol/L
questions.answer: b) No restriction needed unless K+ >5.0 mmol/L
questions.explanation: ACEI/ARB initiation does not require routine potassium restriction unless hyperkalaemia develops (K+ >5.0 mmol/L). Restriction is unnecessary and may cause harm; supplements are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female with NYHA class III HFrEF (EF 25%) is on lisinopril 20 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. She develops persistent dry cough. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate adjustment?
options: a) Stop lisinopril and switch to losartan
questions.answer: a) Stop lisinopril and switch to losartan
questions.explanation: ACEI-induced cough is a common adverse effect; switching to an ARB (e.g., losartan) is appropriate. Reducing carvedilol or stopping spironolactone does not address the cough; increasing lisinopril worsens symptoms.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with hypertension and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 42 mL/min) is started on amlodipine 5 mg daily. Which of the following is the MOST likely adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Amlodipine (CCB) commonly causes peripheral oedema due to vasodilation. Bradycardia and hyperkalaemia are not typical; hypoglycaemia is unrelated.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old female with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 38 mL/min) is started on dabigatran 150 mg BD for stroke prevention. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate advice regarding alcohol consumption?
options: a) Limit to 1 standard drink daily
c) Limit to 2 standard drinks weekly
questions.explanation: Alcohol increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants and worsens renal function in CKD. Avoidance is recommended. Limiting intake does not eliminate risk.

questions.stem:
a) List the four classes of drugs used as first-line antihypertensives according to WHO/KDIGO guidelines. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug and its primary mechanism of action. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four first-line antihypertensive classes are:
   - ACE inhibitors (ACEI)
   - Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB)
   - Calcium channel blockers (CCB)
   - Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics

b) Examples and mechanisms:
   - ACEI (e.g., lisinopril): Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion, leading to vasodilation and natriuresis.
   - ARB (e.g., losartan): Blocks angiotensin II type 1 receptors, preventing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.
   - CCB (e.g., amlodipine): Inhibits calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation.
   - Thiazide (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide): Inhibits sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing diuresis and reducing plasma volume.

questions.stem:
a) Outline the KDIGO-recommended BP targets for patients with CKD and diabetes. (2 marks)
b) List two classes of antihypertensives that provide renoprotective benefits in diabetes. (2 marks)
c) Explain why ACE inhibitors are preferred over ARBs in patients with diabetes and CKD. (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) KDIGO recommends a BP target of <130/80 mmHg for patients with CKD and diabetes to reduce renal and cardiovascular risk.

b) Two renoprotective classes in diabetes:
   - ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril)
   - ARBs (e.g., losartan)

c) ACE inhibitors are preferred over ARBs in diabetes and CKD because they reduce intraglomerular pressure more effectively by blocking angiotensin II formation (not just receptor binding), providing additional renoprotective benefits beyond BP control.

questions.stem:
a) List the four classes of antianginal drugs used in the management of stable angina. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug and its primary mechanism of action. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four classes of antianginal drugs are:
   - Beta-blockers
   - Calcium channel blockers (CCB)
   - Nitrates
   - Ranolazine

b) Examples and mechanisms:
   - Beta-blocker (e.g., metoprolol): Reduces heart rate and contractility, decreasing myocardial oxygen demand.
   - CCB (e.g., amlodipine): Inhibits calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, causing coronary and peripheral vasodilation, reducing afterload and improving coronary perfusion.
   - Nitrate (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate): Releases nitric oxide, causing venous and arterial vasodilation, reducing preload and afterload.
   - Ranolazine: Inhibits late sodium current in cardiac myocytes, reducing diastolic tension and oxygen demand.

questions.stem:
a) List the three main types of heart failure based on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). (1.5 marks)
b) For each type, provide the LVEF range and one example of a guideline-recommended drug therapy. (3.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three main types of heart failure based on LVEF are:
   - Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
   - Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
   - Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (HFmrEF)

b) LVEF ranges and drug therapy:
   - HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%): ACE inhibitor (e.g., lisinopril) + beta-blocker (e.g., carvedilol) + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone).
   - HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%): Diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for volume overload; no specific mortality-reducing therapy proven.
   - HFmrEF (LVEF 41–49%): Treat as HFrEF if symptomatic; consider ACEI/ARB/beta-blocker if tolerated.

questions.stem:
a) List the four classes of antiarrhythmic drugs according to the Vaughan Williams classification. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug and its primary mechanism of action. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four classes of antiarrhythmic drugs (Vaughan Williams classification) are:
   - Class I (sodium channel blockers)
   - Class II (beta-blockers)
   - Class III (potassium channel blockers)
   - Class IV (calcium channel blockers)

b) Examples and mechanisms:
   - Class I (e.g., flecainide): Blocks sodium channels, slowing conduction in cardiac tissue.
   - Class II (e.g., metoprolol): Blocks beta-1 receptors, reducing heart rate and contractility.
   - Class III (e.g., amiodarone): Blocks potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and refractory period.
   - Class IV (e.g., verapamil): Blocks calcium channels, slowing AV node conduction and reducing heart rate.

questions.stem:
a) List the three main types of diuretics used in heart failure. (1.5 marks)
b) For each type, provide one example of a drug and its primary site of action in the nephron. (3 marks)
c) Explain why loop diuretics are preferred over thiazides in acute decompensated heart failure. (0.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three main types of diuretics used in heart failure are:
   - Loop diuretics
   - Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics
   - Potassium-sparing diuretics

b) Examples and sites of action:
   - Loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide): Acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, inhibiting Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransport.
   - Thiazide (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide): Acts on the distal convoluted tubule, inhibiting Na+/Cl- cotransport.
   - Potassium-sparing (e.g., spironolactone): Acts on the collecting duct, blocking aldosterone receptors.

c) Loop diuretics are preferred in acute decompensated heart failure because they produce a more potent diuresis, even in patients with reduced renal function, and are less affected by diuretic resistance.

questions.stem:
a) List the four main classes of drugs used for lipid modification in dyslipidaemia. (2 marks)
b) For each class, provide one example of a drug and its primary mechanism of action. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The four main classes of lipid-modifying drugs are:
   - HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins)
   - Ezetimibe
   - PCSK9 inhibitors
   - Fibrates

b) Examples and mechanisms:
   - Statin (e.g., atorvastatin): Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing LDL receptor expression.
   - Ezetimibe: Inhibits Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 protein, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption.
   - PCSK9 inhibitor (e.g., evolocumab): Binds PCSK9, preventing LDL receptor degradation and increasing LDL clearance.
   - Fibrate (e.g., fenofibrate): Activates PPAR-alpha, increasing lipoprotein lipase activity and reducing triglycerides.

questions.stem:
a) List the three main types of renal replacement therapy (RRT) used in end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). (1.5 marks)
b) For each type, provide one example of a drug that requires dose adjustment in ESKD. (3 marks)
c) Explain why vancomycin requires dose adjustment in ESKD. (0.5 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) The three main types of RRT are:
   - Haemodialysis
   - Peritoneal dialysis
   - Kidney transplantation

b) Examples of drugs requiring dose adjustment in ESKD:
   - Vancomycin (for haemodialysis)
   - Digoxin (for peritoneal dialysis)
   - Metformin (for kidney transplantation)

c) Vancomycin requires dose adjustment in ESKD because it is primarily renally excreted, and accumulation in renal failure increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 45 mL/min) presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and bilateral leg oedema. He reports that he has been non-adherent to his medications for the past 3 weeks due to financial constraints. His current medications include lisinopril 10 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg BD, furosemide 40 mg BD, and metformin 500 mg BD.

On examination:
- BP 168/102 mmHg, HR 110 bpm (irregularly irregular), RR 24/min, SpO₂ 92% on room air
- Jugular venous pressure elevated to 6 cm
- Bibasal crackles on chest auscultation
- Abdomen distended with shifting dullness
- Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin

Investigations:
- Hb 12.8 g/dL, WCC 8.2 x10⁹/L, Plt 210 x10⁹/L
- Na+ 132 mmol/L, K+ 5.1 mmol/L, Creatinine 220 µmol/L (eGFR 28 mL/min), Urea 18.5 mmol/L
- BNP 1200 pg/mL
- ECG: AF with rapid ventricular response, no ST-segment changes
- CXR: Pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly
- Echocardiogram: LVEF 35%, moderate mitral regurgitation, no significant valvular disease


a) What is the most likely diagnosis? Provide a rationale. (3 marks)
b) Outline the immediate management priorities for this patient. (5 marks)
c) Discuss the long-term management plan, including non-pharmacological and pharmacological strategies, to reduce hospital readmissions. (7 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Most likely diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) with volume overload, complicated by atrial fibrillation (AF) with rapid ventricular response and CKD stage 4 (eGFR 28 mL/min).
   Rationale:
   - Progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and bilateral leg oedema suggest volume overload.
   - Elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, and abdominal distension confirm congestive heart failure.
   - AF with rapid ventricular response contributes to worsening heart failure symptoms.
   - Elevated BNP and echocardiogram findings (LVEF 35%, moderate mitral regurgitation) support ADHF.
   - Worsening renal function (eGFR 28 mL/min) is consistent with cardiorenal syndrome.

b) Immediate management priorities:
   - Oxygen therapy (if SpO₂ <90%) to maintain oxygenation.
   - IV furosemide 80–120 mg bolus, followed by continuous infusion if needed, to achieve euvolaemia.
   - Rate control for AF: IV metoprolol or digoxin if beta-blockers contraindicated (e.g., severe bronchospasm). Target HR <100 bpm.
   - Consider IV nitrates (e.g., glyceryl trinitrate) if hypertensive (SBP >140 mmHg) to reduce preload/afterload.
   - Monitor electrolytes (K+, Mg²⁺) and renal function closely due to diuretic use and CKD.
   - Consider IV inotropes (e.g., dobutamine) if hypotensive or cardiogenic shock.
   - Address non-adherence: Provide social work support, medication access programs, or generic alternatives.

c) Long-term management plan:
   Pharmacological strategies:
   - Optimise guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF:
     • ACE inhibitor (e.g., lisinopril) or ARB (e.g., losartan) if ACEI-intolerant.
     • Beta-blocker (e.g., carvedilol) titrated to target dose (e.g., 25 mg BD).
     • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone 25 mg daily) if eGFR >30 mL/min and K+ <5.0 mmol/L.
     • SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g., dapagliflozin 10 mg daily) for additional renal/cardiac protection.
   - Rate/rhythm control for AF:
     • Beta-blocker (e.g., metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine CCB (e.g., diltiazem) for rate control.
     • Consider amiodarone if rhythm control is needed (e.g., post-cardioversion).
   - Anticoagulation for stroke prevention (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 3): DOAC (e.g., apixaban 5 mg BD) if eGFR >25 mL/min.
   - Statin therapy (e.g., atorvastatin 40 mg nocte) for cardiovascular risk reduction.
   - Optimise glycaemic control (e.g., switch metformin to insulin if eGFR <30 mL/min).

   Non-pharmacological strategies:
   - Sodium restriction (<2 g/day) and fluid restriction (<1.5 L/day) to reduce volume overload.
   - Daily weight monitoring and symptom diaries to detect early decompensation.
   - Cardiac rehabilitation program to improve functional capacity and adherence.
   - Patient education on medication adherence, symptom recognition, and self-management.
   - Regular follow-up with cardiology and nephrology to monitor GDMT, renal function, and adjust therapy.
   - Address social determinants of health (e.g., medication access, transportation) to improve adherence.

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old female with a history of hypertension, CKD stage 3 (eGFR 48 mL/min), and AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 4) presents to the clinic for a routine review. She is currently on rivaroxaban 15 mg daily for stroke prevention, amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension, and atorvastatin 20 mg nocte for dyslipidaemia. She reports no symptoms but mentions occasional bruising and fatigue.

On examination:
- BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 72 bpm (irregularly irregular), RR 16/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air
- No signs of volume overload or peripheral oedema
- Mild bruising on forearms

Investigations:
- Hb 11.5 g/dL, WCC 6.8 x10⁹/L, Plt 180 x10⁹/L
- Na+ 138 mmol/L, K+ 4.7 mmol/L, Creatinine 150 µmol/L (eGFR 42 mL/min), Urea 8.2 mmol/L
- INR 1.1 (not on warfarin)
- LFTs normal
- Urinalysis: Proteinuria 1+ (no haematuria)


a) What are the key issues in this patient’s management? (3 marks)
b) Outline a pharmaceutical care plan to address these issues, including monitoring parameters and patient education. (12 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Key issues in this patient’s management:
   - Suboptimal BP control (BP 142/88 mmHg) despite amlodipine, increasing cardiovascular risk.
   - Potential bleeding risk with rivaroxaban (occasional bruising) and CKD stage 3 (eGFR 42 mL/min).
   - Fatigue may be related to anaemia of CKD or drug adverse effects (e.g., statin-induced myalgia).
   - Proteinuria 1+ suggests possible progression of CKD, requiring further evaluation.
   - AF with CHA₂DS₂-VASc score 4 requires optimal stroke prevention and rate/rhythm control.

b) Pharmaceutical care plan:

   Pharmacological optimisation:
   - BP management: Add ACE inhibitor (e.g., lisinopril 5 mg daily) or ARB (e.g., losartan 25 mg daily) to amlodipine for better BP control and renoprotection. Monitor creatinine and K+ at 1–2 weeks.
   - Anticoagulation: Continue rivaroxaban 15 mg daily (appropriate for eGFR 30–59 mL/min) but review bleeding risk. Consider switching to apixaban if bleeding concerns persist (apixaban 5 mg BD is renally adjusted to 2.5 mg BD if eGFR 15–29 mL/min).
   - Statin therapy: Continue atorvastatin 20 mg nocte; monitor LFTs and CK if myalgia develops.
   - Consider SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g., dapagliflozin 10 mg daily) for additional renoprotective and cardioprotective benefits (eGFR 42 mL/min is acceptable).
   - Rate control for AF: Optimise beta-blocker (e.g., metoprolol 25 mg BD) or consider digoxin if beta-blockers are poorly tolerated.

   Monitoring parameters:
   - BP: Weekly home BP monitoring; target <130/80 mmHg.
   - Renal function: eGFR and creatinine every 3–6 months; more frequently if ACEI/ARB initiated.
   - Electrolytes: K+ and Na+ every 3–6 months; more frequently if ACEI/ARB or diuretics initiated.
   - Bleeding risk: Review bruising and any signs of bleeding (e.g., GI bleeding, epistaxis).
   - LFTs and CK: Every 6–12 months or if symptoms of myalgia.
   - AF control: ECG or Holter monitoring if symptoms persist; target HR <100 bpm.

   Patient education:
   - Medication adherence: Emphasise the importance of taking medications as prescribed, including ACEI/ARB, beta-blocker, and anticoagulant.
   - Bleeding precautions: Advise on avoiding NSAIDs, excessive alcohol, and high-risk activities. Report any signs of bleeding (e.g., black stools, prolonged bleeding).
   - BP monitoring: Teach home BP monitoring technique and target values.
   - Lifestyle modifications: Sodium restriction (<2 g/day), fluid restriction if needed, regular exercise, and smoking cessation.
   - Symptom recognition: Educate on signs of decompensated heart failure (e.g., dyspnoea, oedema) and AF (e.g., palpitations, fatigue).
   - Follow-up: Schedule regular clinic visits (every 3–6 months) for medication review and monitoring.

   Additional considerations:
   - Address fatigue: Evaluate for anaemia (e.g., iron studies, B12/folate) if persistent.
   - Proteinuria: Consider nephrology referral for further evaluation (e.g., urine protein-creatinine ratio, renal biopsy if indicated).
   - Social support: Assess for barriers to adherence (e.g., cost, transportation) and provide resources (e.g., medication access programs).
